# Overview: Distributed Transactions

Many business operations change state in more than one place: a ledger in one service, a payout record in another, a notification queue in a third. A transaction in the usual sense is a unit of work that either completes entirely or leaves no trace. Within a single database, the storage engine provides this. Across services, each with its own database and failure modes, nothing provides it automatically. Distributed transaction protocols exist to close that gap, and they make different trade-offs between correctness, availability, and coupling.

The two approaches covered in this section are the two most common answers. **Two-phase commit (2PC)** tries to preserve the classic transaction guarantees across participants. **Sagas** give up on cross-service atomicity and instead guarantee that a failed operation is brought back to a consistent state through explicit compensating actions.

## Two-Phase Commit

In 2PC, a coordinator asks every participant to prepare the transaction. Each participant checks that it can commit, durably records its vote, and holds its locks. If every participant votes yes, the coordinator records a commit decision and tells everyone to commit. If any participant votes no, or fails to respond, the coordinator aborts.

The protocol gives atomicity and, when combined with the participants' local isolation, a strong consistency guarantee. Its cost is the window between prepare and commit. A participant that has voted yes cannot unilaterally commit or abort; it must wait for the coordinator's decision. If the coordinator crashes in that window, the participants hold locks until someone recovers the decision from the coordinator's log. This is the blocking problem, and it is why 2PC is most dependable when the coordinator's log is durable and highly available, and when the participants are databases or resources under one operational umbrella.

Two-phase commit is practical inside one data center or trust boundary, and it is the basis of the XA standard that many database drivers support. It is much less practical across organizations, across high-latency links, or across services that cannot tolerate lock hold times measured in seconds.

## Sagas

A saga breaks a business operation into a sequence of local transactions, each committed in its own database. Every step has a compensating action that semantically undoes it. If step *n* fails, the saga runs the compensations for steps *n-1* down to 1 in reverse order.

Sagas come in two styles. In **orchestration**, a central component holds the workflow and calls each step in turn. In **choreography**, each service publishes an event when its step completes, and the next service reacts to that event. Orchestration is easier to reason about and to monitor, because the sequence lives in one place. Choreography removes the central component but spreads the workflow across services, which makes it harder to see the whole process and to change it safely.

The defining trade-off is isolation. Once a step commits, its effects are visible to other readers before the saga finishes. A customer may see a debit before the matching credit is applied. Sagas therefore need countermeasures: semantic locks that mark records as pending, versioned records that readers can check, and designs that tolerate intermediate states. Compensations also have limits. A refund is not the same as never having charged the card, and a notification that was already sent cannot be recalled. A saga has to accept that some effects are permanent, and it should order its steps so that irreversible actions happen last.

## Comparison

| Concern | Two-phase commit | Saga |
|---|---|---|
| Atomicity | All-or-nothing across participants | Eventual consistency through compensation |
| Isolation | Participants hold locks until the decision | Intermediate states are visible |
| Failure during coordination | Participants may block until recovery | Each step is independent; the workflow resumes from its log |
| Latency | Bounded by the slowest participant and lock hold time | Each step commits quickly; total time is the sum of steps |
| Coupling | Participants must support the protocol | Participants need only idempotent actions and compensations |
| Typical use | Databases in one trust domain; XA resources | Long-running, cross-service business workflows |
| Main design effort | Durable coordinator log; timeout and recovery rules | Compensation design; idempotency; handling of intermediate states |

## Relationship to the Earlier Material

The ideas from the leader election and settlement sections apply directly to both approaches. A saga's steps are retried after timeouts, so every step and every compensation must be idempotent, keyed by a stable identifier. A saga orchestrator that fails over is a leader in the sense covered earlier, so it needs a fencing token at each downstream service to refuse commands from a superseded instance. A 2PC coordinator that recovers its decision from a log has to be single-writer for that log, and its recovery must be fenced the same way. The settlement example's pattern of a resource that records completed work and skips duplicates is effectively a saga step with an idempotency check.

## Choosing Between Them

Use 2PC when the participants are databases that support it, the operation must be atomic with respect to other readers, and the lock hold time is short and bounded. Use a saga when the participants are independent services, when operations are long-running, or when a blocked participant is more harmful than a temporarily visible intermediate state. In most payment and settlement systems the second condition holds, which is why sagas with explicit compensations are the common choice there.

The sections that follow examine each approach in turn: the 2PC protocol and its recovery rules, then saga design, including compensation ordering, semantic locking, and orchestration versus choreography, with the failure cases worked through step by step.

# Core Concepts in Distributed Transactions (2PC and Sagas)

These six concepts account for most of the design decisions and most of the production failures in this area. Each one describes a property that is easy to state and hard to get right under failure.

## 1. The Uncertainty Window in Two-Phase Commit

Once a participant votes yes in the prepare phase, it has promised that it can commit. It has also durably recorded that promise and is holding its locks. From that point until it hears the decision, it cannot safely commit or abort on its own. If it aborted, the coordinator might have decided commit; if it committed, the coordinator might have decided abort. That interval is the uncertainty window, and the participant is blocked for its duration.

The window is not a theoretical concern. A coordinator crash, a network partition between the coordinator and one participant, or a stalled coordinator process all extend it, and the locks the participant holds may block unrelated transactions on the same rows. The standard mitigation is the cooperative termination protocol: a prepared participant asks its peers whether any of them has seen a decision. If one has committed or aborted, the others follow it. If every participant is prepared and none has heard a decision, the protocol cannot make progress, and the system has to wait for the coordinator.

**What a senior engineer checks:** how long locks are held in the prepared state in production, what the timeout policy is, and whether anything resolves in-doubt transactions automatically or requires a human. Lock hold time during a coordinator outage is the number that determines whether 2PC is tolerable for a given system.

## 2. Durable Decision Logging and Recovery

The coordinator's correctness rests on one rule: it must durably record its decision before it tells any participant. A commit decision that exists only in memory is lost on a crash, and participants that were told to commit have no way to learn it from anywhere else. The decision record is the source of truth for every in-doubt participant, so it must be forced to stable storage before phase two begins.

Recovery follows from this. A restarted coordinator reads its log. Transactions with a commit record are re-driven to commit at every participant, and this step must be idempotent, because participants may already have committed. Transactions with no decision record are usually aborted under the presumed-abort convention: if the coordinator has no record of a transaction, it answers any inquiry with abort. Presumed abort keeps the log small, because the coordinator does not need to log aborts, but it depends on the coordinator never forgetting a transaction that might still have been committed.

**What a senior engineer checks:** that the log write is actually forced to disk (not buffered), that the coordinator's log is replicated or otherwise survives the loss of one machine, and that only one coordinator instance can write a given transaction's log. Two coordinators acting on the same transaction after a failover is the coordinator equivalent of split brain, and it is covered by the fencing ideas from the leader election section.

## 3. Compensation Is Semantic, and Step Ordering Determines Recoverability

A compensating action is not a database rollback. It is a new business action that counteracts the effect of an earlier one: a refund for a charge, a cancellation for a reservation, a reversal entry for a posting. The difference matters because the world may have changed between the forward step and the compensation. A rollback that restores a snapshot would overwrite a concurrent update; a semantic compensation applies a delta that remains correct regardless of intervening changes.

Steps in a saga fall into three categories, and the order matters:
- **Compensable steps** can be undone by a later action. They run before the pivot.
- **The pivot** is the step after which the saga is committed to completing. It is the point of no return. It may be an irreversible action, such as sending funds to an external bank.
- **Retriable steps** run after the pivot. They cannot be compensated, so they must eventually succeed, which means they retry until they do.

A compensation can itself fail. For this reason, every compensation must be idempotent and retriable, and the saga needs a defined escalation path when a compensation cannot succeed, usually a manual-intervention queue with the saga's full state attached. A compensation that silently gives up leaves the system inconsistent with no alarm.

**What a senior engineer checks:** that the pivot is identified explicitly for each saga, that irreversible actions sit at or after the pivot, and that every compensation has a tested failure path. A common error is placing a payment before a reservation that can fail, which makes the payment impossible to undo cleanly.

## 4. Isolation Anomalies and Their Countermeasures

Because a saga commits each step locally, other transactions can observe intermediate states. These anomalies are the main source of subtle bugs in saga-based systems:

- **Dirty reads:** a reader sees a debit that a later step will reverse.
- **Lost updates:** a compensation overwrites a concurrent change, if it restores a stale value.
- **Non-repeatable reads:** the same record changes between two reads inside one business operation.

The standard countermeasures are design choices, not library features:
- **Semantic locks:** mark a record as pending, so other operations treat it as unavailable or in-progress until the saga finishes.
- **Commutative updates:** express changes as deltas, so their order does not matter.
- **Pessimistic ordering:** place steps that are likely to fail early, so the saga rarely has to compensate.
- **Version checks:** reread and compare a version before acting on a value that another saga might change.

These countermeasures reduce anomalies but do not remove them. The team must decide, per operation, which anomalies are acceptable and which require a semantic lock.

**What a senior engineer checks:** for each saga, a short written list of the intermediate states it exposes and who can observe them. A saga whose intermediate state can be shown to a customer needs a different design from one whose intermediate state is internal.

## 5. Idempotency and the Dual-Write Problem

Distributed systems deliver messages at least once. A timeout does not tell the sender whether the receiver processed the message, so the sender retries, and the receiver may run the same step twice. Every saga step and every compensation must therefore be idempotent, keyed by a stable identifier such as the saga instance ID combined with the step name.

The related trap is the dual write. A service that updates its database and then publishes an event has two separate writes with no transaction between them. A crash between them loses the event, or publishes one for a change that did not commit. The standard fix is the transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, and have a relay publish from that table. The consumer side uses an inbox table, recording processed message IDs in the same transaction as its effect, so a redelivered message is detected and skipped.

The result is exactly-once effect, achieved from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. Exactly-once delivery is not available in general, and designs that assume it are a common source of duplicated payments.

**What a senior engineer checks:** that every state change that produces an event goes through an outbox, that every consumer has a deduplication record, and that the deduplication record is written in the same transaction as the effect. A consumer that deduplicates in a separate transaction still has a window in which it can act twice.

## 6. Orchestrator Fencing and Superseded Commands

A saga orchestrator holds the workflow state, and it can fail or be replaced like any other leader. Two hazards follow. First, a timed-out command may still complete at the downstream service, so the orchestrator cannot assume that a timeout means the step did not happen. Second, an orchestrator that was replaced may still send commands that were in flight when it lost its role.

The defenses are the ones from the leader election section, applied to commands. Each command carries the saga instance ID and an epoch or attempt number that increases when the orchestrator recovers the saga. Each downstream service records the highest epoch it has accepted for that saga and refuses lower ones. On timeout, the orchestrator must query the step's status rather than assume failure, and it must treat a compensation for a step that never ran as a safe no-op, because the step may have been in flight when the saga was cancelled.

**What a senior engineer checks:** that the orchestrator's persisted state is updated before each command is sent and after each response is received, that recovery reads that state rather than recomputing it, and that downstream services actually enforce the epoch check. The epoch check is the piece most often omitted, because it looks like redundant machinery until the first failover produces a duplicate command.

## Summary

Two-phase commit trades availability for atomicity. Its risks are the uncertainty window and the coordinator's log, and both must be treated as production concerns with measured lock hold times. Sagas trade isolation for availability. Their risks are intermediate states, compensations that cannot be cleanly defined, and duplicate delivery. The concepts above are the questions a senior engineer should be able to answer for any design in this space: how long a participant can be blocked, where the decision lives, which step is the pivot, which intermediate state is visible, how a step is made safe to repeat, and how a superseded orchestrator is prevented from acting.

# Trade-offs in Distributed Transactions, with Failure Stories

The trade-offs in this area are not abstract. Each design choice buys one property and gives up another, and the cost usually appears during a failure, not during normal operation. The scenarios below are illustrative. They are constructed to show recurring failure patterns, not reports of specific incidents at any company. Each one names the trade-off it exposes and the control that would have limited the damage.

## 1. Atomicity versus Availability: The Blocked Ledger

**Scenario.** A payments platform uses 2PC across a ledger database, a payout service, and a notifications store. The coordinator runs on a single VM with a local log. During a routine deploy, the VM fails between the prepare and commit phases for about 40 transactions.

**What happened.** The ledger participants had voted yes and held row locks on the affected merchant accounts. Those locks blocked balance reads for every checkout touching those merchants. The coordinator took 40 minutes to recover, because the replacement VM needed manual steps to attach the log volume. Checkout error rates rose sharply for the whole interval, even for merchants whose transactions had nothing to do with the failure.

**The trade-off.** 2PC bought atomicity across the three stores. The price was that a single coordinator outage held locks in the ledger, and the locks had a blast radius far beyond the in-doubt transactions. The protocol was correct; the operational envelope was not.

**What would have limited it.** A lock timeout policy that aborts in-doubt transactions after a bounded interval under presumed-abort rules, a coordinator deployed with automated failover, and a runbook that named who could resolve in-doubt transactions and how. The lesson the team recorded was that the lock hold time during a coordinator outage was an SLO, and it had never been measured.

## 2. Presumed Abort Depends on the Log Never Being Lost

**Scenario.** A coordinator wrote its decision log to local disk. The disk failed, and the replacement was provisioned from a machine image that did not include the log. The coordinator restarted with an empty log.

**What happened.** Several transactions had been committed at the ledger but were still in progress at the payout service. A participant asked the restarted coordinator about one of them. The coordinator had no record, and under presumed abort it answered abort. The ledger had already committed, so the payout service rolled back, and the two stores disagreed about a payment. The discrepancy surfaced days later in reconciliation.

**The trade-off.** Presumed abort keeps the coordinator's log small, because aborts need not be written. It is correct only if the log is never lost. The optimization removes a write from the common path and makes the log's durability a correctness requirement, not a performance detail.

**What would have limited it.** Replicating the decision log across machines in different failure domains, forcing writes to stable storage, and a restore test that checked the log was present after a simulated disk loss. The question to ask is not whether the log is usually safe but what the system does when it is not.

## 3. Isolation versus Latency: The Double Spend Inside the Window

**Scenario.** A marketplace implemented a payout as a saga: debit the seller's balance, then call the bank, then record the payout. There was no semantic lock on the balance. A seller with a balance of 500 initiated two payouts of 400 within seconds.

**What happened.** The first saga debited the balance, which left 100. The second saga read the balance while the first was still waiting on the bank, saw it as sufficient at the time of its own check, and debited again. The balance went negative, and the bank honored both payouts. The second saga's compensation was then triggered by a bank rejection, but the funds had already left.

**The trade-off.** A saga commits each step immediately, which keeps the database short-lived and avoids holding locks during a slow external call. That same choice exposes intermediate state. Adding a semantic lock or a reservation step would have made the first payout's pending state visible to the second, at the cost of extra steps and extra failure modes to handle.

**What would have limited it.** A reservation step that moves funds into a pending account before the bank call, with a check that is atomic with the reservation. The principle is that any check performed in one saga step must still be true when the next step acts on it, or the check must be made inside the same step.

## 4. Simplicity of Rollback versus Correctness of Compensation

**Scenario.** A booking service implemented compensation by snapshotting a record before a multi-step operation and restoring the snapshot on failure. A customer's loyalty balance was 1,000 points. A forward step deducted 200 points for a booking. While that saga was in flight, a separate process credited 300 points for a referral. The booking then failed, and the compensation restored the snapshot.

**What happened.** The referral credit of 300 was lost. The loyalty balance was reset to 1,000 instead of 1,300. Nothing errored, and the discrepancy was found only when a customer disputed their balance.

**The trade-off.** Snapshot restore is simple to implement and easy to test in isolation. It is wrong whenever another writer can touch the same record during the saga. Semantic compensation, which applies a delta of plus 200 points, is more work to design but remains correct under concurrency.

**What would have limited it.** Expressing both the forward step and its compensation as deltas on the balance, not as absolute values. The rule for reviewers is simple: if a compensation writes an absolute value it has read earlier, it is probably a lost update waiting to happen.

## 5. Automatic Recovery versus Visibility: The Refund That Never Landed

**Scenario.** An order saga charged a card, then reserved inventory, and the reservation failed. The compensation was a refund call to the payment processor. The processor returned 503 errors for nine hours. The compensation worker retried with backoff, but it had no dead-letter path and no alert on the age of pending compensations.

**What happened.** About 2,300 customers were charged for orders that had been canceled. The problem was caught by a daily reconciliation job the next morning. Refunds were issued in bulk, and support handled the complaints for a week.

**The trade-off.** Automatic retry is the right default, because most compensation failures are transient. Without a bound on retries and an alert on the age of outstanding compensations, automatic recovery becomes silent accumulation. The system looked healthy while it was failing.

**What would have limited it.** A dead-letter queue for compensations that exceed a retry budget, an alert on the oldest pending compensation rather than on the error rate, and a dashboard showing the number of sagas in each state. The principle is that every saga must be able to answer the question "what is still outstanding, and since when?"

## 6. Idempotency Cost versus Build Speed: The Duplicate Payout

**Scenario.** An orchestrator called an external bank API to initiate a payout. The bank call timed out after eight seconds. The orchestrator marked the step as failed and retried. The first call had in fact succeeded at the bank, and the bank had processed it.

**What happened.** The seller received two payouts for the same settlement line. The bank's API accepted an idempotency key, but the team had not passed one, because the bank integration predated the team's idempotency standard.

**The trade-off.** Making every external call idempotent takes effort, and that effort is easiest to skip for integrations that look simple. The cost of skipping it is invisible until a timeout happens, and then it is a duplicate financial transfer.

**What would have limited it.** A rule that every external call with side effects must carry a stable key derived from the saga ID and step name, plus a test that injects a timeout after the call succeeds, to confirm the retry produces one effect.

## 7. Centralized Orchestration versus Fencing Complexity

**Scenario.** An orchestrator ran as a primary with a standby. During a network partition, the primary lost its lease. The standby took over and resumed a saga from its persisted state. The primary, unaware it had lost the role, sent a shipment command that was already in its outbound queue.

**What happened.** Two shipment commands reached the warehouse for one order. The warehouse accepted both, because it did not check which orchestrator instance issued each command.

**The trade-off.** Centralized orchestration makes the workflow easy to read and monitor. The price is that the orchestrator is a leader, and every leader problem from the leader election section now applies to every saga. Teams often adopt orchestration without adding epoch checks to downstream services, and the first failover exposes the gap.

**What would have limited it.** Command epochs tied to the orchestrator's lease, and downstream services that record the highest epoch per saga and refuse lower ones.

## 8. Choreographed Decoupling versus Observability

**Scenario.** An onboarding process was implemented as a choreography across six services, each reacting to events. A schema change in one event added a required field. One consumer rejected the new events and logged a warning, which nobody monitored.

**What happened.** About 3,000 onboarding workflows stalled at the same step. No single service showed an error rate high enough to alert on. The team spent three days reconstructing the workflow state from logs in each service.

**The trade-off.** Choreography removes the central coordinator and lets services evolve independently. The cost is that the workflow exists only as the sum of its event handlers, and no single component can report where a given instance is.

**What would have limited it.** A correlation ID carried on every event, a workflow-level view that tracks each instance's last observed step, and alerts on instances that have not advanced within an expected interval. Choreography can be operated well, but it needs observability designed in, not added after the first incident.

## 9. Latency versus Lock Hold Time: The Cross-Region Collapse

**Scenario.** A team ran 2PC across two regions to keep ledger writes strictly atomic. Prepare latency was about 80 milliseconds intra-region and about 900 milliseconds cross-region. Under normal load, the system worked. At peak, lock hold times grew, and throughput fell by more than half.

**What happened.** Each transaction held locks for the full round trip. Contention rose as lock queues grew, which made each transaction slower, which made the queues longer. The team moved the cross-region flows to sagas over several weeks.

**The trade-off.** 2PC's throughput is bounded by lock hold time, and that time grows with the slowest participant's latency. A design that is correct at low load can fail at high load without any component breaking.

**What would have limited it.** Load-testing 2PC with realistic cross-region latency before adoption, and an explicit decision on which flows could tolerate the lock hold time.

## Summary of the Trade-offs

| Trade-off | Buys | Costs | Failure pattern to watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2PC atomicity | All-or-nothing across stores | Lock hold during coordinator outage | Blocked reads during a coordinator failure |
| Presumed abort | Smaller coordinator log | Log durability becomes a correctness requirement | Disagreement after log loss |
| Saga local commits | Short transactions, no locks during slow calls | Visible intermediate state | Double spend inside the window |
| Snapshot rollback | Simple to implement | Lost updates under concurrency | Silently reverted concurrent changes |
| Automatic compensation retry | Recovers from transient failures | Silent accumulation if unbounded | Outstanding work that no alert covers |
| Idempotency everywhere | One effect per logical operation | Engineering effort per integration | Duplicate external effects after a timeout |
| Central orchestrator | Readable, monitorable workflow | Leader-election problems for every saga | Superseded commands acted on |
| Choreography | Independent evolution | Workflow state scattered across services | Stalled instances nobody can see |
| 2PC across regions | Strict atomicity | Throughput bounded by round-trip latency | Throughput collapse under load |

## Guidance for Practitioners

Three questions cover most of the decisions above. First, what happens to the system when a single coordinator, orchestrator, or external call is unavailable for an hour, and how many customers are affected? Second, which intermediate states can be observed, and by whom? Third, how does the team find out that something is outstanding, and how long has it been outstanding?

Systems that answer those three questions well usually choose sagas with semantic compensation, idempotent steps, and explicit outstanding-work views, and they reserve 2PC for participants inside one operational boundary. The failure stories show that the most expensive errors are not the protocol choices themselves but the unmeasured assumptions around them: lock hold time, log durability, compensation age, and whether an external call was actually idempotent.

# Common Mistakes with Distributed Transactions (2PC and Sagas)

These mistakes come up repeatedly in systems that coordinate work across services. The examples are composite patterns, not reports of specific incidents. Each entry describes the mistake, why it hurts, and how to catch it before production does.

## 1. Treating a saga as an atomic rollback

**What it looks like:** The design says "if shipping fails, we roll back the charge," as though the earlier steps never happened.

**Why it hurts:** A compensation is a new business action, not an undo. A refund takes days to settle and may appear on the customer's statement. An email that was already sent cannot be unsent. Between the forward step and its compensation, other parts of the system and the customer may have acted on the intermediate state.

**How to catch it:** For each compensation, write down what the outside world may have observed in the meantime, and whether the compensation is acceptable from the customer's point of view. Review this in design, not after an incident. If a compensation cannot be made acceptable, the step probably belongs after the pivot.

## 2. Non-idempotent steps or compensations

**What it looks like:** A step increments a counter, appends a row, or charges a card without a stable key. A retry after a timeout repeats the effect.

**Why it hurts:** At-least-once delivery means every step can run more than once. Without idempotency, a single timeout produces a double charge or a double reservation.

**How to catch it:** Run every forward step and every compensation twice with the same key, and assert that the effect appears once. The idempotency tests in `dtx_example.py` do this for the reserve step (scenario 3). Apply the same test to every step your system defines, and make it part of CI.

## 3. Compensations that break when they run first

**What it looks like:** The compensation assumes its forward step already ran. A refund finds no charge and fails, or a release finds no reservation and does nothing, then the late forward call succeeds.

**Why it hurts:** Retries and message reordering let a compensation arrive before its forward call. The forward call then applies with no one left to undo it, which holds stock or money for an order that has already been canceled.

**How to catch it:** Test each compensation on an empty state, and then deliver the forward call. The expected result is a refusal. The tombstone in scenario 6 of `dtx_example.py` is the pattern to copy. Compensations should record that the order was canceled, and forward calls should check that record.

## 4. Dual writes between the database and the message bus

**What it looks like:** A service writes its row, then publishes the event or command in a separate step. The two can disagree when the process crashes between them.

**Why it hurts:** A crash after the write and before the publish loses the step entirely. The saga stalls with no visible error. A retry of the whole handler can also write twice.

**How to catch it:** Inject a crash between the database commit and the publish call, and check whether the system recovers. The fix is a transactional outbox: write the event to a table in the same transaction as the state change, and have a relay publish from that table. The test is to kill the process at every point in the handler and check that the outbox and state agree after restart.

## 5. The coordinator's decision is not durable before it is acted on

**What it looks like:** The 2PC coordinator sends commit messages before the decision is written to stable storage, or it keeps the decision only in memory.

**Why it hurts:** If the coordinator crashes after some participants commit and before others hear the decision, the participants that are still prepared hold locks and cannot learn the outcome. If the decision was never persisted, recovery may choose abort for a transaction that some participants already committed. That violates atomicity and cannot be repaired from the coordinator's side.

**How to catch it:** Test the crash points around the decision write, as scenarios 3 and 4 in `dtx_example.py` do. In production, confirm that the decision write is fsynced before the first delivery, and run process-kill tests that stop the coordinator at random points during commit. After each kill, check that every participant reaches the same outcome.

## 6. Misidentifying the pivot

**What it looks like:** A non-retriable step is treated as retriable, or a step after the pivot is treated as compensable. The saga retries a shipment that was refused, or compensates a shipment that already left the warehouse.

**Why it hurts:** Retrying a refused business action keeps failing and never reaches a terminal state. Compensating past the pivot undoes an action the outside world has already accepted, which produces inconsistent state that no compensation can repair.

**How to catch it:** Make the step classification explicit in code, as `STEPS` does in `dtx_example.py`, and write a test that fails each step in turn and checks the resulting path. Review the classification whenever a step is added or its external effect changes.

## 7. Timeouts treated as failures

**What it looks like:** A timeout is interpreted as "the call did not happen," so the orchestrator compensates or retries without knowing the state.

**Why it hurts:** A timeout only means no reply arrived. The effect may already have happened. Compensating without checking can double-undo, and retrying without an idempotency key can double-apply.

**How to catch it:** Inject lost replies on every call: the service applies the effect and then drops the response. Check that the system converges to a single effect. Scenario 3 in the saga part of `dtx_example.py` is a minimal version of this test.

## 8. Unbounded holds in 2PC

**What it looks like:** Prepared participants keep their locks indefinitely while waiting for a decision. Nobody monitors how long a transaction stays in doubt.

**Why it hurts:** Held resources block other transactions. A coordinator outage that lasts minutes can stall unrelated work across the system. Teams often discover this only when a queue backs up.

**How to catch it:** Track the age of the oldest in-doubt transaction on every participant, and alert when it exceeds the expected commit latency by a clear margin. Load-test the coordinator's failure modes, not just its throughput. Consider whether the business can tolerate 2PC for this operation at all. Often a saga with a pivot gives the same guarantee with no cross-service locks.

## 9. Stuck sagas with no sweeper

**What it looks like:** A saga pauses in `retry_later` or `compensating`, and nothing resumes it. The saga table fills with non-terminal rows that no one reads.

**Why it hurts:** Customers see half-finished orders, and the inconsistency stays hidden until someone complains. Manual cleanup is expensive and error-prone.

**How to catch it:** Export a metric for the number of sagas in each non-terminal state and the age of the oldest one. Alert on any saga older than its expected completion time. Run a sweeper that calls `resume` on every non-terminal saga, and test it by leaving a saga paused on purpose and checking that it completes.

## 10. Orchestrator takeover without fencing

**What it looks like:** After a failover, the old orchestrator is still running and sends commands alongside the new one.

**Why it hurts:** Both orchestrators issue commands for the same saga. Without fencing, the stale one can apply a step or compensation that conflicts with the new one's decision.

**How to catch it:** Test takeover explicitly: start a saga on orchestrator A, pause A, start B on the same saga, then resume A and check that its commands are rejected. Fencing with epochs, as in the earlier worked example, is the standard defense.

## 11. Exposing intermediate states without a plan

**What it looks like:** The user interface or another service reads the order as "confirmed" while the saga is still running. It later changes to "canceled."

**Why it hurts:** Customers and downstream systems act on states that were never final. This is the saga version of a dirty read, and it creates support work that a correct final state would have avoided.

**How to catch it:** List the states a saga passes through, and mark which ones are visible to readers. Use explicit pending states, and decide what each reader should do with them. Test with reads running concurrently with the saga, and check that no reader sees a state it cannot handle.

## 12. Testing only the happy path

**What it looks like:** The test suite covers the successful run and perhaps one failure. Crash points, lost replies, and out-of-order delivery are never exercised.

**Why it hurts:** Most of the bugs in this list appear only under partial failure. The happy path passes regardless of whether compensations are idempotent or the outbox is correct.

**How to catch it:** Build a failure matrix with one row per step and one column per fault type: business refusal, transient failure, lost reply, crash before and after the step, and duplicate delivery. Run randomized schedules of crashes and delays across many seeds, and check invariants after each run. The invariants to check are that every saga reaches a terminal state, that money and stock balance, and that no effect appears twice.

## 13. No reconciliation

**What it looks like:** The system trusts its own state machine. Nothing independently checks whether, for example, charges match shipments.

**Why it hurts:** Some bugs will get through every test. Without an independent check, they persist until a customer or an auditor finds them, which can take months.

**How to catch it:** Run a reconciliation job that compares the state of each service against the others. Examples: every shipped order has a charge, every canceled order has no open reservation, every charge older than the saga timeout has a terminal saga. Treat any mismatch as a bug and alert on it.

## Summary of Detection Methods

| Mistake | Primary detection |
|---|---|
| Atomic-rollback assumption | Design review of each compensation's visible effects |
| Non-idempotent steps | Duplicate-delivery tests with the same key |
| Compensation before forward call | Out-of-order tests with tombstone checks |
| Dual writes | Crash injection between database commit and publish; outbox check |
| Non-durable decision | Process-kill tests around the decision write |
| Misidentified pivot | Failure test at every step index; classification review |
| Timeout as failure | Lost-reply injection on every call |
| Unbounded 2PC holds | Age-of-in-doubt metric and alert |
| Stuck sagas | Non-terminal state metrics and sweeper tests |
| Missing fencing | Takeover test with the stale orchestrator resumed |
| Exposed intermediate states | Concurrent reads during saga execution |
| Happy-path-only testing | Failure matrix and randomized fault schedules |
| No reconciliation | Cross-service invariant job with alerts |

The common thread is that most of these mistakes are invisible under normal operation. The defenses are fault injection, explicit invariants, and monitoring for non-terminal states, which together turn silent inconsistency into a visible failure. The `dtx_example.py` file covers the idempotency, tombstone, pivot, and recovery tests, but the outbox, sweeper, fencing, and reconciliation checks in this list still need to be built around any real implementation.

# Distributed Transactions Compared with Alternatives

The main question is not which protocol is best but whether the operation needs a distributed transaction at all. Several alternatives remove the need entirely, and others keep the transaction but change how it commits. The comparison below covers the approaches most often weighed against 2PC and Sagas.

## The alternatives

**1. Avoid the distributed transaction (single database or co-location).** Keep the data that must change together in one database, or in one shard. A transaction then runs inside a single engine with full ACID guarantees. Teams often reach for 2PC or Sagas because two services were split for organizational reasons, not because the data requires it. If the order and the ledger entry can share a shard keyed by customer, the problem goes away.

**2. Try-Confirm-Cancel (TCC).** Each participant exposes three operations. *Try* reserves resources without committing them, *Confirm* makes the reservation final, and *Cancel* releases it. A coordinator calls Try on every participant, then Confirm if all succeed or Cancel if any fail. Unlike a 2PC prepare, the reservation is a business-level hold that the service defines itself, and it has an expiry so that abandoned reservations free up.

**3. Eventual consistency with reconciliation.** Each service commits its own local transaction and publishes events. A reconciliation job compares the services and repairs or flags mismatches. There is no cross-service atomicity and no cross-service compensation chain. Correctness depends on the reconciliation logic and on operations that tolerate temporary disagreement.

**4. Convergent, commutative designs (CRDTs, append-only ledgers).** Design the data so that updates can be applied in any order and any number of times with the same result. An append-only ledger where the balance is derived from entries, or a counter that merges by addition, needs no coordination across writers. The result is convergence without any protocol at all, but only for operations that are naturally commutative.

**5. Consensus-backed commit (Spanner-style, Raft-replicated participants).** The 2PC participants are themselves replicated groups that run consensus, and the coordinator's state is replicated too. A coordinator crash then no longer blocks prepared transactions, because another replica can take over with the same decision state. This addresses the blocking problem of plain 2PC at the cost of much more infrastructure.

**6. Deterministic ordering (Calvin-style).** Transactions are sequenced into a global order before execution, and every replica runs them in the same order. Distributed commit becomes unnecessary because each node knows what every other node will do. The cost is that the transaction's read and write sets must be known up front.

## Comparison

| Dimension | 2PC | Sagas | Single-DB / co-location | TCC | Eventual + reconciliation | Convergent designs | Consensus-backed 2PC | Deterministic ordering |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomicity | Yes, all or nothing | No, compensated eventually | Yes | Yes, via business holds | No, repaired later | Not needed, converges | Yes | Yes |
| Isolation | Holds block others | Intermediate states visible | Full | Holds visible as pending | None across services | Not applicable | Holds block others | Serial order |
| Behavior under coordinator failure | Blocks until recovery | Resumes from saga state | N/A | Needs timeout and sweeper | Not applicable | Not applicable | Replica takes over | Sequencer must recover |
| Latency | Multiple round trips, holds locks | Sequential steps | Lowest | Two phases of business calls | Lowest across services | Lowest | Higher, consensus rounds | Batching adds delay |
| Service coupling | Tight, shared protocol | Moderate, orchestrator knows steps | Shared database | High, each service implements three ops | Low | Low | Infrastructure coupling | High, shared sequencer |
| Implementation effort | Protocol and log | Steps, compensations, state | Little, if co-located | Three operations per service | Reconciliation and monitoring | Data model redesign | Specialized infrastructure | Specialized infrastructure |
| Failure visibility | Stuck in-doubt transactions | Non-terminal sagas | Errors surface immediately | Expired holds | Mismatches found later | Hard to see | Infrastructure alarms | Sequencer health |
| Fits when | Few participants, short holds, trusted resource managers | Long-running steps, external effects, pivot exists | Data can share a boundary | Business reservations are natural | Temporary inconsistency is acceptable | Operations are commutative | Need atomicity without blocking | Workload is predictable and known up front |

## Trade-offs in practice

**Co-location is usually the cheapest option, and it is often overlooked.** The cost is a constraint on the partitioning scheme: operations that span partitions become rarer and more expensive, and the design must accept that. If most transactions can stay within one partition, the distributed protocol is a rare path and its complexity can be contained. If they cannot, the choice shifts toward the other alternatives.

**TCC sits between 2PC and Sagas.** It gives atomicity without holding database locks across services, because the hold is a business object instead of a prepared transaction. The price is that every participant must implement three operations and handle expiry. TCC works well when a reservation has a natural meaning, such as a seat or a stock unit. It works poorly when the operation has no business-level hold to express.

**Reconciliation is often the right answer for high-volume, low-stakes effects.** Notifications, analytics, and loyalty points are common examples. Teams sometimes apply saga machinery to these, which adds state and failure modes without adding value. The question to ask is what a mismatch costs and how long it can persist before anyone notices.

**Consensus-backed commit addresses the main weakness of 2PC, but not the cost of coordination.** Replicating the coordinator removes the case where the decision is lost with one machine, but every commit still pays for consensus rounds across the participants. This makes sense when the system already runs a replicated database, and it is hard to justify when it does not.

**Deterministic ordering changes the problem rather than solving it.** Once transactions are sequenced, the sequencer becomes the bottleneck and a single point of coordination. The approach fits workloads with predictable access patterns, such as batch processing. It fits poorly with interactive transactions whose read and write sets depend on runtime results.

**Convergent designs require a different data model.** A ledger that stores entries rather than balances converges without coordination, but reads of the current balance must aggregate entries, and some business rules (for example, a balance that must never go negative) cannot be enforced without coordination at all. The constraint that matters has to be checked before the design is chosen.

## Decision guidance

Start with the question of whether the data must change together. If it can share a boundary, use one transaction and stop there.

If the operation crosses boundaries and the effects are internal to systems you control, choose between 2PC and Sagas based on how long the steps take and whether they have external effects. Short, internal, lock-friendly steps suit 2PC. Long steps or steps with external effects suit a saga with a clearly marked pivot.

If the business has a natural reservation concept, consider TCC before a saga, because it lets the reservation be visible and expire on its own.

If the effects are low-stakes or commutative, choose eventual consistency with reconciliation or a convergent design, and spend the effort on monitoring.

If the system already runs consensus-replicated state, consensus-backed commit may be the cheapest way to avoid blocking. If it does not, the infrastructure cost is hard to justify for this decision alone.

Deterministic ordering is worth considering only for workloads whose access patterns are known in advance.

These are general patterns and the trade-offs above are qualitative. Latency and throughput depend heavily on the network, the hardware, and the workload, so measure the candidates against the real operation before committing to one.

# Distributed Transactions FAQ (2PC and Sagas)

**1. When should a team choose a distributed transaction at all, rather than redesigning the data so one transaction suffices?**

Almost always the redesign should come first. A distributed transaction is justified only when the data that must change together genuinely cannot share a boundary, such as a single database or a single shard. Before choosing 2PC or a saga, check whether the operation can be co-located by a partition key that the business already uses, like a customer or an account. If it can, a local ACID transaction gives full atomicity and isolation with far less machinery, and the distributed path becomes a rare fallback for the operations that really do cross the boundary.

The other reason to distribute is organizational: two services owned by different teams. That is a legitimate reason, but it does not make the transaction problem disappear. It only means the team boundary is paying for complexity that the data model did not require. If the split is the real constraint, the protocol choice should follow from the business semantics described in the comparison section, not from a default preference for one protocol.

**2. What is the practical difference between 2PC and a saga when something fails in the middle?**

With 2PC, the outcome is decided by a single commit point. Before the decision is logged, a failure leads to abort, and all participants release their holds. After the decision is logged, the outcome is commit, and recovery must eventually deliver it to every participant. Participants that have voted yes hold their resources until they learn the decision, so a coordinator outage blocks them. Nothing becomes visible to other transactions until commit, so the isolation story is clean, but the cost is blocking.

With a saga, a failure before the pivot triggers compensations that run in reverse order. Each completed step is undone by a new business action, such as a refund or a release. Between the forward step and its compensation, the intermediate state is visible to readers and to other services. Nothing blocks at the database level, but the customer may see a charge and a refund rather than no charge at all. After the pivot, the saga does not compensate; it retries until it completes.

In short, 2PC trades availability and latency for atomic visibility, and a saga trades visibility for availability and bounded resource holds.

**3. What do idempotency keys and the saga's durable state each protect against, and does one make the other unnecessary?**

They protect against different failures and are not substitutes. The durable state, meaning the saga table or the 2PC decision log, protects against the orchestrator losing its memory. When a crash happens, a new instance reads the state and resumes from the last recorded step, instead of guessing what happened.

Idempotency keys protect against the same request being applied more than once. Timeouts and lost replies make this unavoidable, because the caller cannot tell whether a call took effect. A stable key, such as the saga identifier combined with the step name, lets the service return the stored result on a retry rather than applying the effect again.

Durable state without idempotency still double-applies: the orchestrator resumes and resends a step whose reply was lost. Idempotency without durable state still loses progress: the retry works, but nothing records which step should come next after a crash. Both are required for correct recovery.

**4. How do I know whether a compensation is acceptable, and what if it is not?**

A compensation is acceptable when the business can live with the visible history that remains. Ask two questions for each one. First, what could the outside world have observed between the forward step and its compensation? A customer may have seen a charge, a confirmation email may have been sent, or a warehouse may have started packing. Second, is the reversal a faithful business action, such as a refund with a record, or does it hide the original event? Good compensations leave an audit trail that shows what happened and why it was reversed.

If a compensation is not acceptable, the usual answer is to move the step after the pivot. The pivot is the last step whose effect cannot be undone, and steps after it are retried until they complete. Sometimes the right choice is to restructure the operation so the irreversible action happens last, after every reversible check has passed. If neither works, the operation may need a reservation with an expiry, as in TCC, so that the pending state is explicit to readers and resolves on its own.

**5. How do I test that a distributed transaction is correct before it reaches production?**

Happy-path tests are not enough, because most defects appear only under partial failure. Build a failure matrix with one row per step and one column per fault: business refusal, transient failure, lost reply, crash before the step, crash after the step, and duplicate delivery. For each cell, run the operation and check the same invariants: every saga or transaction reaches a terminal state, money and inventory balance, no effect appears twice, and compensations leave no residual holds. Add out-of-order tests that deliver a compensation before its forward call and check that a tombstone blocks the late forward call.

For the coordinator and orchestrator, add process-kill tests that stop them at random points, then restart them from durable state and check that every participant reaches the same outcome. For takeover, pause the old orchestrator, start a new one on the same saga, resume the old one, and confirm that its stale commands are rejected. Run randomized schedules of crashes and delays across many seeds, and treat any violated invariant as a failing test.

Finally, add reconciliation checks that run in production. Compare the states of the services against each other, for example that every shipped order has a charge and that no reservation remains open for a canceled order. Tests catch the failures you imagined, and reconciliation catches the ones you did not.

# Executive Summary: Distributed Transactions (2PC and Sagas)

**Purpose.** When one business operation changes data in more than one system, the company needs a way to keep those systems consistent when things fail partway through. This summary explains the two main approaches, the trade-offs between them, and the decisions leadership should make before a team commits to either.

**The core problem.** A customer order might reserve stock, charge a card, schedule shipping, and send a confirmation. Any of those steps can fail after others have succeeded, and networks time out without revealing whether a request was processed. Without a deliberate design, the result is inconsistent records: customers charged for items that never ship, or stock held for orders that were canceled.

**The two approaches.**

- **Two-phase commit (2PC)** coordinates all participants so that the operation either completes everywhere or nowhere. Participants first confirm they can perform the change and hold the resources, then the coordinator records a final decision and every participant applies it. The guarantee is strong. The cost is that participants hold resources while waiting for the decision, so a coordinator outage can block unrelated work. It fits short, internal operations across systems the company controls.

- **Sagas** break the operation into a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action that reverses it. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone with new business actions such as refunds. Nothing blocks at the database level, so sagas tolerate slow or unreliable services well. The cost is that customers and other systems can see intermediate states, and some actions cannot be cleanly reversed. Sagas fit long-running operations, operations with external effects such as emails or shipments, and any operation that has a clear point of no return.

**Alternatives that may be better.** Before choosing either approach, leadership should ask whether the transaction needs to be distributed. Three alternatives often make the problem smaller:

- **Co-locating data** so that operations which must be atomic share one database or one partition. This is usually the cheapest option and should be the default question.
- **Try-Confirm-Cancel**, which reserves resources through business-level holds that expire on their own. It gives atomicity without holding database locks across services, at the cost of more work per service.
- **Eventual consistency with reconciliation** for low-stakes effects, where a periodic job detects and corrects mismatches. This suits notifications and analytics, but it is not appropriate for money or inventory without strong controls.

**Where the risk lies.** Most failures in this area are silent. The common causes are: compensations assumed to be a rollback when they are new business actions; operations that are not idempotent, so retries duplicate effects; dual writes between a database and a message bus, which lose events on crashes; stuck operations that nothing monitors; and testing that covers only the success path. Each of these is preventable with specific engineering practices, but none is caught by ordinary testing.

**Recommended decisions for leadership.**

1. **Require a justification for distribution.** Any proposal for a cross-service transaction should first explain why the data cannot share a boundary. Make co-location the default and require a documented reason to deviate.

2. **Choose the protocol per operation, based on business semantics.** Short, internal, lock-friendly operations may use 2PC. Long or externally visible operations should use a saga with a clearly marked point of no return. The choice should be recorded in the design, not left to the implementer.

3. **Fund the supporting infrastructure, not just the protocol.** A correct implementation needs a durable log or state table, an outbox for reliable event publishing, idempotency keys for every step, and sweepers that resume stuck work. Budget for these up front.

4. **Require failure testing and production monitoring as acceptance criteria.** Each distributed transaction should pass a failure matrix covering lost replies, crashes at every step, and duplicate delivery. Production should alert on the age of unfinished operations and run reconciliation checks across services.

5. **Assign ownership for stuck and inconsistent operations.** Someone must be responsible for the queue of operations that cannot complete automatically, with a defined response time.

**Bottom line.** Distributed transactions are sometimes unavoidable, but they carry real operational cost that is easy to underestimate. The most effective lever is reducing how often they are needed. When they are needed, 2PC and sagas are both viable, and the right choice depends on how long the operation runs, whether it has external effects, and how much blocking the business can tolerate. The decisions that matter most are made at design time: where the boundaries lie, which steps are irreversible, and how the system will show that an operation is stuck.

# Closing: Distributed Transactions (2PC and Sagas)

Distributed transactions exist because one business operation sometimes has to change data that lives in more than one place, and failures can strike between those changes. Both protocols in this section answer that problem, but they answer it differently, and the difference shapes everything else about how a system behaves under failure.

Two-phase commit gives atomicity by making a single coordinator the authority on the outcome. Participants promise to commit before the decision is made, and the decision is written to durable storage before anyone is told. That write is the commit point. Its strength is clear visibility: at any moment, the outcome is either pending or decided, and no reader sees a half-finished state. Its weakness is blocking. A participant that has voted yes must wait for the decision, and the coordinator's failure can hold resources indefinitely.

Sagas give eventual consistency by replacing atomicity with a sequence of local steps and compensations. Their strength is availability: no resource is held across the whole operation, and a slow or failed service does not freeze the others. Their weakness is visibility. Intermediate states are real, compensations are new business actions rather than rollbacks, and the design must mark a pivot after which the saga only moves forward.

## What carries forward

Three ideas from this section will matter in every later topic.

**Durable state is the source of truth for recovery.** The 2PC decision log and the saga's persisted step state are what allow a new process to finish work that a crashed process started. Any system that makes decisions across failures needs a place where those decisions survive the process that made them.

**Idempotency and fencing solve different problems.** Idempotency keys ensure that a repeated request has one effect. Epochs or fencing tokens ensure that a superseded process cannot act at all. Both appeared in the worked examples, and both depend on the same discipline: every command carries enough identity for the receiver to decide whether it is current and whether it is new.

**Failure testing is part of the design.** The most common mistakes in this area, such as compensations that break when they run first, non-durable decisions, and dual writes, are invisible under normal operation. A failure matrix, crash injection, and reconciliation are how a team learns whether the design holds.

The leader election section raised the same concern from another direction. A single coordinator is a single point of failure, and the protections against that, such as leases, fencing, and consensus, are the same tools that make a 2PC decision survive a crash.
